findings: Occasional premature atrial complexes, benign. No sustained arrhythmia, no pauses greater than 2 seconds, no AV block.
cardiac_monitoring.impression: 24-hour Holter monitor with only benign findings.
cardiac_monitoring.rhythm_summary: Predominant sinus rhythm throughout the recording

csf.interpretation: Unremarkable CSF. Normal cell count, protein, and glucose.

ct.impression: No acute intracranial abnormality. No haemorrhage, mass, hydrocephalus, or large-territory infarct.

findings: Structurally normal heart. No intracardiac thrombus or vegetation. No pericardial effusion.

contraindications: Ergotamine and other ergot derivatives: contraindicated during breastfeeding (infant ergotism; suppression of prolactin and milk supply).
output.formulary_status: Sumatriptan, ibuprofen, amitriptyline and propranolol: on formulary.
interactions: Paracetamol (current): no clinically significant interaction with sumatriptan, ibuprofen, amitriptyline or propranolol.
Amitriptyline with sumatriptan: both serotonergic; serotonin syndrome is rare with this combination; counsel on symptoms.
output.proposed: Sumatriptan, ibuprofen, amitriptyline, propranolol; breastfeeding mother, infant aged 6 months
output.summary: No interaction with the current paracetamol. Sumatriptan, ibuprofen, low-dose amitriptyline and propranolol have low milk transfer; ergot derivatives are contraindicated during breastfeeding. Source: LactMed (NIH), MHRA Drug Safety Update 2024.
warnings: Sumatriptan: low milk levels and low oral bioavailability in the infant; breastfeeding need not be interrupted (LactMed).
Ibuprofen: very low milk levels; preferred NSAID during breastfeeding (LactMed).
Amitriptyline: low milk levels at usual doses; no adverse effects reported in most exposed infants; monitor the infant for drowsiness and feeding (LactMed).
Propranolol: low milk levels; considered compatible; monitor the infant for bradycardia and lethargy (LactMed).
Topiramate: passes into milk; diarrhoea and drowsiness reported in some infants, monitor if used. In a woman who can become pregnant it requires the pregnancy prevention programme (MHRA 2024).
Valproate: not to be used for migraine prevention in a woman who can become pregnant (MHRA 2024).
Aspirin at analgesic doses: avoid during breastfeeding (theoretical risk of Reye syndrome and platelet effects in the infant).

output.query: migraine acute and preventive treatment during breastfeeding

results.finding: Paracetamol, ibuprofen and sumatriptan reach low concentrations in breast milk and are acceptable acute treatments during breastfeeding.
results.source: LactMed, National Library of Medicine (sumatriptan, ibuprofen, paracetamol entries)

results.finding: Amitriptyline at low doses and propranolol produce low infant exposure; they are commonly used preventives in nursing mothers, with infant monitoring for drowsiness or bradycardia.
results.source: LactMed, National Library of Medicine (amitriptyline, propranolol entries)

results.finding: Ergot alkaloids can cause ergotism in the infant and suppress lactation; avoid during breastfeeding.
results.source: LactMed, National Library of Medicine (ergotamine entry)

results.finding: Review of acute and preventive migraine drugs in lactation; paracetamol, ibuprofen and sumatriptan are first-line acute options, and propranolol and low-dose tricyclics are preferred preventives.
results.source: Hutchinson S et al. Use of common migraine treatments in breast-feeding women: a summary of recommendations. Headache 2013;53:614-627

output.summary: Paracetamol, ibuprofen and sumatriptan are acceptable acute options during breastfeeding; propranolol and low-dose amitriptyline are the usual preventives in nursing mothers; ergot alkaloids are avoided.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: More than 40 identical attacks over 4 years; unilateral positive visual aura spreading over 20-25 minutes and followed by unilateral migraine headache; 5 of 6 criterion C characteristics; normal examination and no SNNOOP10 red flag
action_criteria.label: Take a structured headache/aura history, neurological examination and red-flag review; apply every ICHD-3 1.2 criterion explicitly
action_criteria.rationale: Migraine with aura is a clinical diagnosis: the history must show at least two attacks and at least three of the six criterion C characteristics, and the examination and red-flag review decide whether any test is needed. Here the attacks are identical for 4 years and the examination is normal, so no imaging is indicated.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Breastfeeding-compatible choices identified: sumatriptan and ibuprofen for attacks, low-dose amitriptyline or propranolol if prevention is chosen; ergots excluded while nursing
action_criteria.label: Check lactation safety and interactions of the proposed acute and preventive migraine drugs
action_criteria.rationale: She is breastfeeding a 6-month-old, so every acute and preventive drug has to be chosen for infant exposure; this changes management (no ergots, no valproate, topiramate only with infant monitoring and the pregnancy prevention programme).

action_criteria.expected_evidence: General lactation evidence for migraine drugs; it does not change the diagnosis
action_criteria.label: Optionally search the literature on migraine treatment during breastfeeding
action_criteria.rationale: Not a clinical step: the diagnosis rests on the history and examination, and the lactation question is answered by the drug check.

prohibited_recommendations: Do not continue or start combined hormonal contraception (pill, patch or ring): migraine with aura is UKMEC category 4; offer a progestogen-only method or an IUD.
Do not prescribe ergotamine or other ergot derivatives while she is breastfeeding.
Do not offer valproate for migraine prevention: she can become pregnant and is not under a pregnancy prevention programme (MHRA 2024).
Do not advise stopping or interrupting breastfeeding to take sumatriptan, ibuprofen or low-dose amitriptyline.
required_recommendations: Diagnose migraine with typical aura (ICHD-3 1.2.1) with a postpartum and menstrually related rise in attack frequency; no imaging is needed (identical attacks for 4 years, normal examination, no red flag).

Acute plan compatible with breastfeeding: sumatriptan 50 mg with ibuprofen 400 mg (or paracetamol 1000 mg) at headache onset rather than during the aura, plus metoclopramide 10 mg for nausea or vomiting; breastfeeding need not be interrupted.

Discuss preventive treatment, since two severe attacks a month with vomiting reach the AHS 2021 threshold to consider it: low-dose amitriptyline 10 mg at night (effective before; monitor the infant for drowsiness) or propranolol are breastfeeding-compatible options.

Counsel on contraception: combined hormonal methods are UKMEC category 4 because of the aura; the progestogen-only pill, implant or levonorgestrel IUS (UKMEC 2) or a copper IUD (UKMEC 1) are suitable while breastfeeding.
Keep a headache diary recording attacks, menstrual days and acute-drug days, and review in about 3 months; keep triptan use under 10 days a month to avoid medication overuse.

avoided_actions.rationale: Head CT is less sensitive than MRI for migraine-relevant structural causes and is not indicated in typical migraine with aura; even when imaging is warranted, MRI is preferred
Lumbar puncture is not indicated in migraine with aura; it is reserved for suspected subarachnoid haemorrhage, meningitis or raised or low intracranial pressure, none of which is suggested here
Routine transthoracic or bubble echocardiography (PFO screening) is not indicated in migraine with aura; PFO closure did not meet its migraine end points in MIST, PRIMA and PREMIUM
Ambulatory cardiac monitoring is not indicated in typical migraine with aura — no role unless cardioembolic stroke is on the differential

accepted: Migraine with typical visual aura (ICHD-3 1.2.1), postpartum exacerbation with menstrually-related pattern

differential.key_features: Excluded as the main diagnosis: every attack has a stereotyped, gradually spreading visual aura before the headache

Postpartum is a risk period, highest in the first weeks; against: 6 months postpartum, attacks identical to the 4 years before pregnancy, headache-free between attacks, no papilloedema, normal examination
Requires marked hypertension and encephalopathy; blood pressure 114/70 and normal mental status
Acute thunderclap headache with visual field loss or ophthalmoplegia; here recurrent stereotyped attacks with full fields between them

key_clinical_evidence: Four years of identical attacks: unilateral flickering visual aura expanding over 20-25 minutes, followed by unilateral migraine headache; 5 of 6 ICHD-3 criterion C characteristics and a normal examination.

Frequency rose from one to two attacks a month after menses resumed and she returned to work, with one attack still perimenstrual; the attack character is unchanged and there is no red flag, so no imaging is needed.
Breastfeeding a 6-month-old: acute and preventive drugs are chosen for low infant exposure (LactMed), ergots are excluded, and combined hormonal contraception is UKMEC category 4 because of the aura.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: At 6 months postpartum, with attacks identical to the 4-year pre-pregnancy pattern, normal blood pressure, no papilloedema and a normal examination, the rise in frequency reflects menses resuming, sleep loss and the return to work, not a new secondary headache
red_herrings.data_point: Headache attacks more frequent in the postpartum period
red_herrings.intended_effect: May anchor on postpartum cerebral venous sinus thrombosis or PRES and prompt imaging

findings.result: More than 40 stereotyped attacks over 4 years; monthly before pregnancy, occasional during pregnancy, two a month for the last 3 months; every attack identical.
Visual only: bright flickering arc in one hemifield that expands and clears; transient blurred vision in the same hemifield during the aura. No sensory, speech, motor or brainstem symptoms.
Gradual expansion; total duration 20-25 minutes; fully reversible.
Unilateral headache, usually right-sided, 7-8/10, follows the aura; nausea, photophobia, occasional vomiting; lasts 6-8 hours.
One attack a month within 2-3 days of menstruation onset (menses resumed 3 months after delivery); 6 months postpartum, breastfeeding.
Paracetamol 1000 mg on about 2 days a month, partial relief; no medication overuse.
Normal: full visual fields to confrontation, no papilloedema, normal power, reflexes, sensation, coordination and gait.

Systemic symptoms: absent. Neoplasia or immunosuppression: absent. Neurological deficit outside the aura: absent. Sudden or thunderclap onset: absent. Onset after 50: absent (onset at 26). Pattern change: frequency rose, character unchanged. Positional or Valsalva trigger: absent. Papilloedema: absent. Puerperium (first 6 weeks): absent (6 months postpartum). Painful eye: absent.

clinical_assessment.impression: ICHD-3 1.2.1 criteria met: recurrent fully reversible visual aura with 5 of 6 criterion C characteristics, followed by migraine headache. No sustained deficit, no change in aura character and no SNNOOP10 red flag.

scores.ICHD-3 criterion C characteristics met: 5 of 6 (at least 3 required): spread, duration, unilateral, positive, headache within 60 min; no succession

patient.chief_complaint: Monthly 'flashing lights' before a headache — 4 years, now more frequent

family_history: Sister has migraine with aura; no family history of stroke or coagulopathy

social_history.note: Software consultant (returned from maternity leave); breastfeeding 6-month-old; non-smoker; no alcohol currently (breastfeeding)

patient.history_present_illness:
A 30-year-old Indian woman presented to the neurology clinic with a 4-year history of monthly episodes consisting of 'flashing lights' followed by a severe headache. She describes the visual phenomenon as seeing a bright flickering arc in one side of her vision that expands and then disappears over about 20-25 minutes. She sometimes cannot see clearly on the affected side during this time. The visual disturbance is then followed by a severe unilateral headache (usually right-sided, 7-8/10) with nausea, photophobia, and occasional vomiting lasting 6-8 hours. She has been taking paracetamol (acetaminophen) 1000 mg with only partial relief.

Before her pregnancy the episodes occurred monthly and were particularly associated with her menstrual cycle (occurring within 2-3 days of the start of her period). She had only occasional attacks during the pregnancy. Her periods returned 3 months after delivery, and over the past 3 months, since she returned to work from maternity leave, the frequency has increased from once to twice monthly, with one attack each month still falling within 2-3 days of the start of her period. Her sister also has migraines. She is breastfeeding her 6-month-old infant and is not on any contraception. She mentions using low-dose amitriptyline 10 mg at night for 3 months, prescribed at a different doctor's office about 18 months ago, which helped, but she stopped it when she became pregnant. She specifically reports all episodes are identical; there are no 'different' episodes and no neurological symptoms between attacks.
